content: Aloe vera is a perennial succulent plant resembling a cactus, classified under the Liliaceae family, and is commonly cultivated in tropical regions. Research conducted on animals has suggested that Aloe vera may have properties that accelerate the wound healing process. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of Aloe vera-based products, such as dressings and topical gels, on the healing of acute wounds (e.g., lacerations, surgical incisions, and burns) and chronic wounds (e.g., infected wounds, arterial ulcers, and venous ulcers). To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Ovid AMED, and EBSCO CINAHL, up to September 2011. No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effectiveness of Aloe vera or Aloe vera-derived products, either alone or in combination with other dressings, for treating acute or chronic wounds. The primary outcomes measured were the proportion of completely healed wounds and the time required for complete healing. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, extracted the data, and assessed the risk of bias, with a third reviewer verifying the process. Seven trials, involving a total of 347 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Five of these trials investigated the effects of Aloe vera on acute wounds, including burns, post-haemorrhoidectomy wounds, and skin biopsy sites. In the case of burns, Aloe vera mucilage did not demonstrate superior healing compared to silver sulfadiazine (risk ratio [RR] 1.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 2.85). However, a reduction in healing time was observed in haemorrhoidectomy patients treated with Aloe vera (mean reduction of 16.33 days, 95% CI 3.46 to 77.15). For skin biopsy wounds, there was no significant difference in the proportion of patients who achieved complete healing during follow-up. In chronic wounds, one trial assessed the effect of Aloe vera on pressure ulcers and found no statistically significant improvement in healing (RR 0.10, 95% CI -1.59 to 1.79). Another trial examining surgical wounds healing by secondary intention reported that Aloe vera significantly delayed the healing process (mean delay of 30 days, 95% CI 7.59 to 52.41). Due to the clinical heterogeneity of the included studies, a meta-analysis could not be performed. Furthermore, the overall quality of the trials was poor, with a high risk of bias, necessitating caution in interpreting the results. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient high-quality clinical evidence to support the use of Aloe vera-based topical agents or dressings for the treatment of acute or chronic wounds.
